CellProof: radiation breaks DNA and a damaged cell does not always die. An AI reads the papers, an exact solver checks every rule, and the few candidate gene changes that remain are hypotheses for the lab.

    The papers

    The AI reads papers. You can hand it more.

    Part one: the papers the AI found and read on its own. Part two: a PDF you give it, for a paper it cannot reach. Each paper becomes a graph of what it says, and the solver judges every link it can.

    Drop a PDF here or click to choose one
    Some papers sit behind a login.

    If you have access, you can hand the PDF to the AI: it is read like the others, the solver judges its links, and its graph appears here. That part runs on your computer, because a web page has no key and no solver.

    python -m cellproof.cli serve

    Only drop papers you may process. Its text goes to the Meta Model API to be read; the PDF and everything read from it stay on this computer.

        The search engine

        Every change of one or two genes. Tried.

        Ask for a cell that dies and nothing else. The solver tries every set of one or two genes, off or on, and keeps the smallest that work. Then pick a tumour profile and ask again.

          In short

          What this is, and what it isn't.

          • Every candidate is checked exactly by a solver, and every number on this page is computed from files in the repository.
          • !It is a model of a cell, not of a person: no treatment, no dose, no medical advice. Hypotheses for the lab.
          • !On outcomes it never saw, the model is no better than the published one. We show that too, outcome by outcome.

LimitsWhat this does not show.
          Words used here, in plain language
          Gene
          A switch inside the cell. In the model every gene is either on or off. (A few molecules that behave the same way are called genes here too.)
          Model
          A published map of the genes and which of them switch which others on or off (Gupta and colleagues, 2023). It is a logic circuit, not a simulation of a real cell.
          Rule
          For each gene, the condition that switches it on, written as a small formula: ! means not, & means and, | means or.
          End state
          A pattern of on and off genes that no longer changes. Each one is something the cell can end up as. (Also called a stable state, a fixed point or an attractor.)
          Fate
          What an end state means for the cell: a pause (arrest), a permanent stop (senescence), self-recycling (autophagy) or programmed death (apoptosis).
          Claim
          One sentence from a paper saying that one gene turns another on or off.
          Link
          A claim turned into a connection between two genes (also called an edge). A change to the model is a link written into a rule.
          Known result
          A lab result from the base paper that the model must reproduce (tests V01 to V10). Every proposed change is tested against all ten.
          Checker
          An exact solver: a program that works through every possibility instead of guessing. It cannot read papers; the AI cannot check exactly.
          Counterexample
          A concrete case the checker found where a rule fails: which test, what was expected and what appeared instead.
          Knock out, force on
          Switch a gene permanently off (like deleting it) or permanently on (like over-producing it) in the model.
          Audit
          Results from papers the AI never read, kept back and scored at the end: the one test it could not have learned from.
          Quote found
          The sentence the AI quoted occurs word for word in the paper. It shows faithful copying, not correct understanding.
          Token
          A short chunk of text. Language models read, write and are billed in tokens.

          The cell

          A damaged cell can pause, age, recycle itself or die.

          This is the published model plus the four genes (kinases) the AI added. Switch DNA damage on, click a gene to switch it off or force it on, and see what the cell can become. Every outcome shown is worked out exactly; none is simulated.

          The agent

          Read, write a rule, check, repair.

          AI models read well but guess with confidence. Solvers check exactly but cannot read. CellProof gives each the job it is good at, and records every step.

          Where the claims go

          Most of what a paper says does not become a rule. Each stage below removes what cannot or should not be used.

          Case files

          Watch a rule get judged.

          Every change the AI suggested has a file: the papers behind it, the rule it became, what the checker said and, when the answer was no, how the AI tried to fix it. Pick the first rejected one to watch the whole loop.

          Limits

          What this does not show.

          CellProof ranks hypotheses for lab testing. It gives no medical advice and makes no clinical claim.

          Built this week: everything in this repository except the published base model (Gupta et al. 2023, CC BY), the open-access papers and the open-source solvers and libraries listed in THIRD_PARTY.md.
